title: The Morning Brief: FIFA's inner circle splits as the Dodgers land Skubal
dek: Two senior FIFA officials broke publicly with Gianni Infantino over a private equity plan for the World Cup, while the baseball trade deadline reshaped several rotations, headlined by the Dodgers landing Tarik Skubal.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The FIFA governance fight and the baseball trade deadline both moved fast this weekend, and neither is resolved: FIFA's power structure is being tested in real time, and several of the new rosters won't be judged until games are played.
bottom_line: The weekend's theme was institutional and roster speed outpacing the usual process, from FIFA's open internal revolt over Gianni Infantino's private equity plan to a baseball trade deadline that sent Tarik Skubal to the Dodgers and reshuffled several other rotations. The FIFA reporting documents resignations, confederation threats, and public accusations of deception, but does not establish whether Infantino's position is actually at risk. The baseball moves are documented in full, including salaries, records, and prospects exchanged, but their competitive impact will only be tested in games still to come. Watch the November 18 FIFA challenger deadline, confederation responses in the coming weeks, and how the newly acquired players perform for their new teams.
body: The single thread running through the weekend is speed: institutions and front offices moving faster than the usual process, and reporting racing to keep up. FIFA president Gianni Infantino went, in the span of about 72 hours, from what the reporting describes as an unassailable position to the center of an open internal revolt. At the same time, Major League Baseball's trade deadline produced a wave of moves that reshuffled contenders' rotations and bullpens overnight.

On the FIFA side, Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker and ex-U.S. Soccer president who had worked alongside Infantino for five years, resigned as FIFA's presidential adviser on Friday in protest of a plan to spin off FIFA's commercial businesses, including the men's and women's World Cups and Club World Cups, into a subsidiary valued at $20 billion, with 20 percent owned by private investors anchored by a New York investment firm tied to Joshua Kushner. Kevin Lamour, FIFA's chief operating officer since 2024, went further in a public statement, saying staff had been deceived by Infantino's handling of the proposal and that he would accept losing his job rather than see it advance. Per BBC reporting cited in the desk's coverage, UEFA threatened Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions, including the World Cup, and CONCACAF called for a full review of FIFA's leadership; the Asian Football Confederation has also distanced itself from Infantino.

In baseball, the Dodgers acquired two-time American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal from the Detroit Tigers late Saturday, sending outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith to Detroit. Skubal, 29, will be a free agent after the season and joins a Los Angeles rotation that, through Friday, had allowed just 411 runs, the fewest in baseball. Elsewhere, the Pittsburgh Pirates acquired reliever Camilo Doval from the Yankees for minor league catcher Omar Alfonzo and outfielder Luis Cruz, with New York covering part of his remaining salary; Doval carries a 4.54 ERA in 44 outings this season after a 2.77 ERA run in San Francisco from 2021 through 2023. The Chicago White Sox acquired right-hander Luis Castillo from the Seattle Mariners, sending reliever Seranthony Dominguez, outfielder Nolan Jones, and catching prospect Boston Smith to Seattle in the four-player deal; Castillo is 3-9 with a 5.06 ERA over 17 starts this year, his worst season by the numbers after a 3.54 ERA campaign last year and a 3.65 career mark over 10 seasons.

Away from the two headline threads, the WNBA's midseason deadline produced its first move, with the Toronto Tempo acquiring forward Aneesah Morrow from the Connecticut Sun for the rights to Maria Kliundikova and a 2028 second-round pick. The Atlanta Falcons signed left guard Matthew Bergeron to a four-year extension worth $96 million with $60 million designated up front in the deal, locking in a starter who has played 49 games since being drafted in 2023. And Oregon State women's basketball players filed a petition for union representation with the Oregon Employment Relations Board, the first college athlete organizing effort built solely on public sector state labor law rather than federal jurisdiction, backed by the United College Athletes Association and more than 100 signed authorization cards.

On the why: the FIFA reporting attributes the crisis to Infantino appearing to negotiate the private equity plan without informing his own organization, which triggered the defections described above. On the baseball side, the reporting frames each trade around win-now calculus against expiring contracts and underperforming veterans, though none of the stories forecast how the new pieces will perform in their new places. The Oregon State filing is explained as a deliberate legal strategy, an attempt to root organizing rights in state rather than federal law, precisely because that pathway is untested.
Desk boards were not available this run, so figures above reflect the reporting as published, not a live tape.

The coming days carry several concrete checkpoints. On FIFA, watch whether Infantino responds directly to Cordeiro and Lamour, whether other officials or confederations add their names to the criticism, and whether the November 18 deadline for presidential challengers draws a serious candidacy. On baseball, Sunday's WNBA midseason trade deadline could bring more deals following the Morrow trade, and the performance of Skubal, Castillo, and Doval in their new uniforms will be an early test of each front office's bet. On the union front, watch for the Oregon Employment Relations Board's initial response to the petition and whether other public university programs consider the same state-law approach.
